speeches.reason: The speech is about financial education, technology and community development. Its only economic content is a passing reference to the Survey of Consumer Finances and job-skill anxieties.

speeches.speaker: FOMC (statement)
speeches.title: FOMC statement
speeches.reason: The 50bp intermeeting cut, with the Committee calling activity 'unacceptably weak' and keeping a weakness-weighted bias, is clearly easing. However, markets already priced substantial cuts, so the move was largely expected; only the intermeeting timing and strong wording tilt it modestly dovish versus expectations.

speeches.speaker: Roger W Ferguson

speeches.reason: Mostly a speech on transparency, but the closing section backs the April 18 easing and the weakness-weighted risk assessment: "it is too early to have a strong conviction that the economy is reaching the end of this period of quite slow growth." He gives no sign of a pause and stresses capital investment and equity wealth risks, but this largely restates the FOMC statement already priced in.

speeches.speaker: Robert D. McTeer

speeches.reason: This is a savings bond campaign talk about household and national saving. It says nothing about the policy path, inflation or near-term rates. The one macro remark, that consumers should not 'get the saving religion too abruptly' given 'current fragile economic circumstances', is a passing aside and not a policy signal.

speeches.speaker: Robert D. McTeer
speeches.title: Remarks before The Friday Group
speeches.reason: The speech is mostly about the New Economy, the tech stock bubble and productivity, with no comment on the near-term rate path. It notes that 'cyclical productivity is likely to suffer' as labor-market slack grows, a mild dovish tilt, but this is offset by the optimistic supply-side view of a 'higher noninflationary speed limit'.

speeches.speaker: William J McDonough
speeches.title: The role of financial stability
speeches.reason: The speech covers bank supervision, the Basel capital accord, market discipline and management of international financial crises. It gives no view on US interest rates, inflation or the US economy; the only macro mention is a passing reference to 'signs of strain associated with the global slowdown in growth'.

speeches.speaker: Laurence H Meyer
speeches.title: Controlling the safety net
speeches.reason: The speech is entirely about bank supervision and the federal safety net: deposit insurance, Basel capital standards, market discipline and the systemic risk exception. speeches.speaker: Alan Greenspan
speeches.title: The financial safety net

speeches.speaker: Robert D. McTeer

This signals the easing cycle is nearing its end, a slightly hawkish tilt relative to the expected path, though he does not call for tightening.

speeches.reason: Meyer sees "some downside risks" to the consensus recovery and says growth will stay sluggish into Q3, which tilts dovish. He also warns that easing must not "create conditions that would lead to higher inflation as the expansion gathers momentum," which offsets it. speeches.speaker: Roger W Ferguson

speeches.reason: The speech is entirely about bank supervision and risk management at community and regional banks (funding sources, securitization recourse, internal controls, Basel II). It says nothing about the outlook for interest rates, inflation or the economy that bears on monetary policy.

speeches.speaker: Mark W Olson
speeches.title: The European Union's financial services action plan
speeches.reason: The testimony covers the EU Financial Services Action Plan, Basel capital rules, accounting standards and national treatment for banks. It says nothing about US interest rates, inflation or the economic outlook that bears on monetary policy.

speeches.speaker: Susan Schmidt Bies
speeches.title: Lessons to be re?learned from recent breakdowns in corporate accounting
speeches.reason: The speech covers accounting, auditing, corporate governance and Basel II disclosure after Enron. It says nothing about the outlook for interest rates, inflation or growth, so it has no bearing on monetary policy. It stresses that "sound accounting, auditing, and disclosure... have long been at the heart of efficient markets."

speeches.speaker: Susan Schmidt Bies
speeches.title: Bank performance and corporate governance
speeches.reason: The speech is mostly about bank performance, risk management, governance and discount window reform. Its only policy content restates that the Fed has "moved from a policy bias to address weakness, to one where the risks of inflation and weakness are balanced," and it says she will not forecast rates. She also states the discount window proposal implies no change in policy stance.

speeches.speaker: Susan Schmidt Bies
speeches.title: Banking supervision and its application in developing countries
speeches.reason: The speech covers bank supervision frameworks and their application in developing countries. It says nothing about US interest rates, inflation or the economy, so it has no bearing on monetary policy.

speeches.speaker: FOMC (statement)
speeches.title: FOMC statement
speeches.reason: The Fed held rates and kept the balanced-risks language, as widely expected, with no dissents. The statement noted that final demand growth and inventory support have moderated and that the strengthening is uncertain. This is a slightly softer growth tone than markets, which priced hikes, may have hoped for, so there is a mild dovish tilt.

speeches.speaker: Edward M Gramlich
speeches.title: One-country and multi-country monetary policy issues
speeches.reason: This is an introductory speech for a research conference, listing open research questions on inflation dynamics, exchange rates, currency regimes, currency unions and policy coordination. It says nothing about the US rate, inflation or growth outlook. He even notes that 'policymakers will not raise or lower rates' because of these conferences.

speeches.speaker: Mark W Olson
speeches.title: Financial markets regulation in the United States
speeches.reason: The speech is about financial regulation: technology, industry consolidation, the shift to risk-based supervision, and the Fed's role under Gramm-Leach-Bliley. It says nothing about inflation, growth, or the path of interest rates.

speeches.speaker: Alan Greenspan
speeches.title: Semi-annual monetary policy report to the US Congress
speeches.reason: Greenspan says the accommodative stance 'likely will not prove compatible over time' with price stability, but 'we have chosen to maintain that stance' because inflation is contained with 'few signs that upward pressures are likely to develop any time soon'. He stresses lingering uncertainty, weak equities, corporate governance problems and cautious business, which pushes the hiking horizon furthe

speeches.speaker: FOMC (statement)
speeches.title: FOMC statement
speeches.reason: The Fed held rates unchanged with no dissents and kept the balance of risks tilted toward economic weakness, as expected. The statement adds that demand softening has been 'prolonged' and stresses financial market weakness, a slightly dovish emphasis. It stops short of signalling an imminent cut, and markets already priced a very low-rate path.

speeches.speaker: Alan Greenspan
speeches.title: Economic volatility
speeches.reason: The speech is a retrospective on volatility, equity premiums and asset bubbles. It argues that 'no low-risk, low-cost, incremental monetary tightening exists that can reliably deflate a bubble', so the Fed should not tighten preemptively and should instead 'mitigate the fallout'. It gives no guidance on the near-term rate path, so the only tilt is a mild dovish one from the case against preemptive

speeches.speaker: William J McDonough
speeches.title: Completing the journey to the New Basel Accord
speeches.reason: The speech is entirely about the Basel Committee's New Capital Accord: its goals, the open issues (complexity, procyclicality, operational risk), the QIS 3 timetable and supervisory readiness. It says nothing about the US interest rate, inflation or growth outlook, so it has no bearing on monetary policy.

speeches.speaker: Robert D. McTeer
speeches.title: Remarks before the National Association for Business Economics, 44th Annual Meeting
speeches.reason: McTeer stresses weak demand, slack in labor and product markets, anemic job growth and a 1.3% Q2 GDP rate, and calls inflation low and 'disinflationary' with deflation a possible risk. He says 'faster real growth is essential' and that 'a policy to promote growth is consistent with a policy to combat deflation', which leans easy. He does not explicitly call for a cut.

speeches.speaker: FOMC (statement)
speeches.title: FOMC statement
speeches.reason: The Fed held rates and kept the 'risks weighted toward economic weakness' language, which was expected. But two dissents (Gramlich and McTeer) favored a cut, a dovish surprise relative to the hold that markets mostly priced. The statement also stressed geopolitical risks and uncertainty about the pickup, which leans easier.

speeches.speaker: Alan Greenspan
speeches.title: Policy coordination
speeches.reason: The speech is a ceremonial address at the opening of the HM Treasury building. It covers the history of US-UK central banking ties, international coordination forums, and London's role as a financial center. It says nothing about the US rate, inflation or growth outlook.

speeches.speaker: Roger W Ferguson
speeches.title: The proposed check clearing for the 21st Century Act
speeches.reason: The testimony is about H.R. 5414, the Check Clearing for the 21st Century Act, covering check truncation, substitute checks, and the Fed's authority over the payments system. It says nothing about the outlook for interest rates, inflation or the economy.

speeches.speaker: Susan Schmidt Bies
speeches.title: Bank performance and corporate governance
speeches.reason: The speech is mostly about bank supervision and governance. It only restates that the Fed's bias has shifted back to 'a concern about economic growth'. She says explicitly 'I am not about to forecast interest rates', and her warning that a rising-rate environment 'should not be overlooked' is advice to bankers, not a policy signal.

speeches.speaker: William J McDonough
speeches.title: Issues in corporate governance
speeches.reason: The speech is about corporate governance, executive compensation, accounting and disclosure. It says nothing about the outlook for rates, inflation or growth that bears on monetary policy. The only macro mention is that past economic performance 'lulled investors into a false sense of security', which is not a policy signal.

speeches.speaker: Roger W Ferguson
speeches.title: Business continuity after September 11
speeches.reason: The speech covers business continuity and disaster recovery for financial market infrastructure after September 11. It discusses a regulators' white paper, sound practices, testing and regional diversification, and says nothing about interest rates, inflation or the economic outlook.

speeches.speaker: Alan Greenspan
speeches.title: The continued strength of the U.S. banking system
speeches.reason: The speech is about why U.S. banks stayed strong through the credit cycle, covering risk management, derivatives, credit scoring and Basel II. It gives no outlook for interest rates, inflation or growth that bears on monetary policy. The only policy-adjacent remarks are about the housing and mortgage market supporting consumers, which is background and not guidance.

speeches.speaker: Susan Schmidt Bies
speeches.title: Corporate governance and risk management
speeches.reason: The speech is about corporate governance, enterprise risk management, internal controls and disclosure. Its only reference to rate-setting is a passing line that Board members do more than "helping to set short-term interest rates". It says nothing about the outlook for inflation, growth or policy.

speeches.speaker: Roger W Ferguson
speeches.title: Central banks and markets
speeches.reason: The speech is mostly about the central bank's role, limits of monetary policy, asset prices and communication. It gives no view on the near-term rate path. The remarks that policy offsets are 'only partial and not necessarily synchronous' and that lags are unpredictable carry a slight dovish tinge, but they refer to last year's shock.

speeches.speaker: Ben S Bernanke
speeches.title: Asset-price ¿bubbles¿ and monetary policy
speeches.reason: This is a conceptual talk on whether monetary policy should respond to asset-price bubbles, with a historical case study of the 1920s. It makes no comment on the current outlook for rates, inflation or growth, and Bernanke says the views are his alone. The framework argument against bubble-popping gives no signal about the policy path.

speeches.speaker: William J McDonough
speeches.title: Promoting financial resilience
speeches.reason: The speech covers Basel II capital rules, corporate accounting standards, and how to manage international (emerging market) financial crises. It says nothing about the US interest rate, inflation, or growth outlook, so it has no bearing on monetary policy.

speeches.speaker: Robert D. McTeer
speeches.title: Remarks before the Cato Institute 20th Annual Monetary Conference, cosponsored with The Economist
speeches.reason: The speech is about banking stability, Basel II, corporate governance and creative destruction. Its only macro remarks are passing ones, such as 'a credit crunch is not the main element of 50 mph head winds this time around' and a note that the recovery is jobless. None of these say anything about the path for interest rates.

speeches.speaker: Robert D. McTeer
speeches.title: Problems Making the Case for the Market: Good Intentions or Good Results
speeches.reason: The speech is mostly about the morality of markets, free trade and economic education. Its only policy-relevant remark is that inflation is low and "poised to go lower, given the slack in the economy, the sluggish recovery and continued productivity growth." That is a slightly dovish tilt, but it sets out no path and dismisses deflation worries with a joke.

speeches.speaker: Alan Greenspan
speeches.title: Productivity
speeches.reason: Greenspan gives a technical account of the productivity surge. He stresses "tepid demand and a virtual disappearance of pricing power", and says that productivity optimism "may currently seem a bit out of place" given the difficult adjustments underway. There is no explicit signal on the rate path, and higher structural productivity is mildly disinflationary, so the tilt is slightly dovish.

speeches.speaker: Roger W Ferguson
speeches.title: Productivity growth - a realistic assessment
speeches.reason: The speech is about trend productivity growth, and Ferguson is "cautiously optimistic" about strong productivity-led growth. He notes the high-tech capital overhang is a drag and that profit recovery is a risk, but says he does not attach a high probability to it. He says nothing about the policy path, so it is balanced and close to neutral.

speeches.speaker: FOMC (statement)
speeches.title: FOMC statement
speeches.reason: The 50bp cut was larger than the 25bp many expected, though bill yields suggested a sizable chance of it. The statement's shift to balanced risks signals the easing cycle may be ending, which offsets the larger-than-expected cut, so the net tilt is slightly dovish.

speeches.speaker: Susan Schmidt Bies
speeches.title: Effective accounting and disclosure for financial transactions and financial institutions
speeches.reason: The speech is about accounting, auditing, disclosure and corporate governance after Enron and Sarbanes-Oxley. It says nothing about the outlook for interest rates, inflation or the economy. Typical lines include "disclosure practices should evolve from sound risk management" and "what we need is to restore the integrity of corporate governance, company accountants, and the audit process."

speeches.speaker: Roger W Ferguson
speeches.title: Economic progress and small business
speeches.reason: The speech is mostly about minority wealth and small business, with a brief monetary policy passage. It defends last week's easing as meant to keep the recovery 'on track and not be derailed by the recent soft spot', and notes the labor market recovery is 'very slow'. That restates the FOMC view with a slight dovish tilt and no new path signal.

speeches.speaker: Mark W Olson
speeches.title: The banking industry in 2002 after a decade of change
speeches.reason: The speech reviews the banking and thrift industries over the past decade, covering consolidation, profitability, asset quality, and internal controls. It says nothing about the outlook for interest rates, inflation, or monetary policy. The only passing mentions of 'low interest rates' and 'recent economic weakness' are about bank earnings, not the policy path.

speeches.speaker: Susan Schmidt Bies
speeches.title: North American monetary policy - key developments in recent times
speeches.reason: Bies mostly restates the FOMC statement. She describes the economy as passing through a 'soft spot', the current policy stance as adequate, and risks as balanced. She adds that the Fed 'remains vigilant' and ready to change policy, and she gives no signal of further easing or tightening.

speeches.speaker: Alan Greenspan
speeches.title: The wealth of nations revisited
speeches.reason: This is a historical and academic talk on the sources of long-run growth (openness, institutions, macroeconomic stability). It says nothing about the US rate outlook, near-term inflation or the economy. The remark that 'Controlling inflation is essential to creating an environment of sustained growth' is a general principle, not a policy signal.

speeches.speaker: Alan Greenspan
speeches.title: The economic outlook
speeches.reason: Greenspan says the economy 'has hit a soft patch', with households cautious, business spending lacking vigor and risk spreads wider. He also says firms cannot raise prices, so inflation is contained. He mostly restates the FOMC statement and signals no new easing, so the dovish tilt is slight.

speeches.speaker: Alan Greenspan
speeches.title: International financial risk management
speeches.reason: The speech covers international finance, risk dispersion, derivatives, central banks as lenders of last resort, and regulation. It gives no outlook on US rates, inflation or the economy beyond noting that the economy 'is still growing' despite shocks, so it carries no policy-path signal.

speeches.speaker: Roger W Ferguson
speeches.title: Financial engineering and financial stability
speeches.reason: The speech is about financial engineering and financial stability: dynamic hedging of mortgages, herding from risk models, and credit derivatives. It says nothing about the outlook for interest rates, inflation or growth that bears on monetary policy.

speeches.speaker: Ben S Bernanke
speeches.title: Deflation - making sure 'it' doesn't happen here

speeches.speaker: Robert D. McTeer
speeches.title: Reflections and Confessions of an Erstwhile Economist
speeches.reason: This is a mostly autobiographical and historical talk with no explicit guidance on the rate path. It mentions a sluggish, jobless recovery, strong productivity, and a fondness for money growth consistent with policy, plus ironic remarks that nobody worries about liquidity traps. These are balanced and do not signal a change from the expected path.

speeches.speaker: FOMC (statement)
speeches.title: FOMC statement
speeches.reason: The Fed held rates and kept the balanced risk assessment, which markets expected after the November cut and its shift to balanced risks. speeches.speaker: Mark W Olson
speeches.title: The importance of market structure
speeches.reason: The speech covers bank consolidation, antitrust analysis, deposit insurance reform and small business credit. It says nothing about the outlook for interest rates, inflation or the economy that bears on monetary policy.

speeches.speaker: Laurence H Meyer
speeches.title: Financial Stability in Emerging Markets - What Have We Accomplished and What Remains To Be Done?
speeches.reason: The speech reviews emerging-market financial stability. It covers exchange rate regimes, debt management, standards and codes, IMF reform and private-sector involvement in debt restructuring. It says nothing about the US interest rate, inflation or growth outlook.

speeches.speaker: Alan Greenspan
speeches.title: Issues for monetary policy

He describes the economy as in a 'soft patch', with a subdued labor market, weak manufacturing and a 'lack of pricing power', and says the U.S. is 'nowhere close' to deflation. He also stresses resilience and that productivity-led growth should pick up. This is a mildly dovish rest

speeches.speaker: Edward M Gramlich
speeches.title: Conducting monetary policy
speeches.reason: Gramlich explicitly declines to discuss the current economy or his likely vote, and gives a general talk on strategy: a long-run price stability anchor, short-term flexibility, and being 'ahead of the curve'. Mild dovish tilt from stressing symmetric responses to deflation and readiness to 'change interest rates quite quickly', but no new signal on the path.

speeches.speaker: Ben S Bernanke
speeches.title: ¿Constrained discretion¿ and monetary policy
speeches.reason: This is a conceptual speech on the 'constrained discretion' framework and the history of the Great Inflation. It says nothing about the near-term rate path or the current outlook. It stresses commitment to price stability and 'strict avoidance of deflation as well as of inflation', which is balanced, and it notes that the 2001 easing did not unanchor inflation expectations.

speeches.speaker: William J McDonough
speeches.title: Risk management, supervision and the New Basel Accord
speeches.reason: The speech is entirely about risk management, bank supervision and the New Basel Accord. It says nothing about the outlook for interest rates, inflation or the economy that bears on monetary policy. The only macro reference is a passing mention of 'the recession that began early last year' when discussing problem banks.

speeches.speaker: Roger W Ferguson
speeches.title: September 11, the Federal Reserve, and the financial system
speeches.reason: The speech is a historical review of the Fed's liquidity, payment-system and financial-stability response to September 11, 2001. It mentions the 50bp cut on September 17, 2001 only as past history and says nothing about the current outlook for rates, inflation or growth.

speeches.speaker: William J McDonough
speeches.title: Implementing the New Basel Accord
speeches.reason: The speech covers the New Basel Accord, its implementation, risk management and supervisory approaches. It says nothing about US interest rates, inflation or the economic outlook.

speeches.speaker: Susan S Bies
speeches.title: Financial markets and corporate governance in the United States and other countries
speeches.reason: The speech covers corporate governance, accounting and disclosure, financial innovation, and bank-based versus market-based financial systems in Germany, Japan and the US. It contains no discussion of the outlook for interest rates, inflation, or the economy that bears on monetary policy.

speeches.speaker: Alan Greenspan
speeches.title: Federal Reserve Board's semiannual monetary policy report to the Congress
speeches.reason: Greenspan describes a soft labor market, subpar growth and weak business outlays, and says conventional monetary and fiscal stimulus would move higher on the agenda if the economy stays weak. He still sees faster growth as the "more probable expectation" and signals no change in the path. The rest of the testimony is on fiscal policy and is neutral for rates.

speeches.speaker: Roger W Ferguson
speeches.title: Rules and flexibility in monetary policy
speeches.reason: This is a conceptual speech on rules versus discretion and does not give a near-term rate outlook. It says deflation risks in the US are 'minimal' and that 'further aggressive monetary and, in all probability, fiscal stimulus would be brought to bear' if deflation threatened, which is slightly dovish. It also stresses commitment to price stability, so the net tilt is roughly neutral.

speeches.speaker: Ben S Bernanke
speeches.title: Balance sheets and the recovery
speeches.reason: Bernanke gives an upbeat view that household, bank and corporate balance sheets are strong enough to support an 'increasingly robust economic recovery' in 2003-04. He does not comment on the policy path. He notes uncertainty over Iraq and a labor market that is 'stable' but not robust, so the tilt is only slightly hawkish relative to expectations.

speeches.speaker: Alan Greenspan
speeches.title: Deposit insurance
speeches.reason: The testimony covers FDIC reform proposals: merging BIF and SAIF, risk-based premiums, reserve ratio ranges, and opposing a higher coverage ceiling. It has no comment on inflation, growth, or the policy path, so it carries no monetary policy signal.

speeches.speaker: Roger W Ferguson
speeches.title: Basel II
speeches.reason: The testimony covers only the Basel II bank capital standard: A-IRB, operational risk, commercial real estate and competitive equity. It says nothing about US interest rates, inflation or the economic outlook, so it has no monetary policy content.

speeches.speaker: Susan S Bies
speeches.title: Retirement savings, equity ownership, and challenges to investors
speeches.reason: The speech covers 401(k) plan design, household equity ownership and proxy-voting disclosure. It says nothing about interest rates, inflation or the economic outlook that bears on monetary policy.

speeches.speaker: Alan Greenspan
speeches.title: Aging global population
speeches.reason: This is long-run testimony on demographics, Social Security and Medicare, labor force participation and productivity. It says nothing about near-term inflation, the economic outlook or the policy rate, so it has no bearing on the monetary policy path.

speeches.speaker: Donald L Kohn
speeches.title: The strength in consumer durables and housing: policy stabilization or problem in the making?
speeches.reason: Kohn defends the aggressive easing and says housing and durables show no dangerous imbalances, so there is no case for tightening early. He treats future tightening as 'inevitable' once business investment recovers, and says the Fed would 'set rates lower than the markets have built in' if markets overshoot. That is a mild dovish tilt, though it is mostly a backward-looking defense of policy.

speeches.speaker: Alan Greenspan
speeches.title: Home mortgage market
speeches.reason: The speech is mostly a descriptive account of mortgage refinancing and home equity extraction. It expects equity extraction to 'appreciably simmer down in 2003', which could ease support for consumer spending. It also says a housing bubble is unlikely and that rising rates would only come with a stronger economy. It gives no guidance on the policy path.

speeches.speaker: Alan Greenspan
speeches.title: Global finance - is it slowing?
speeches.reason: The speech is a structural discussion of financial globalization, derivatives innovation, home bias and capital flows. It says nothing about the near-term outlook for US rates, inflation or growth. The only macro remark, on the widening current account deficit, is historical and not about policy.

speeches.title: Remarks before the Risk Management Association

He also notes the real funds rate is roughly comparable to the 1990s trough. He does not call for cuts and expects no double

speeches.speaker: Ben S Bernanke
speeches.title: A perspective on inflation targeting
speeches.reason: The speech is about the inflation-targeting framework and says nothing on the near-term rate path or the economic outlook. It leans slightly dovish: it says oil price increases "are more likely to promote consideration of increased policy ease", it stresses the dual mandate, and it notes the Fed cut rates by nearly 500bp without hurting inflation expectations.

speeches.speaker: Alan Greenspan
speeches.title: Financial education
speeches.reason: The speech is about financial education and consumer finance trends, such as household debt growth, bankruptcies and mortgage lending practices. It says nothing about the outlook for interest rates, inflation or monetary policy.

speeches.speaker: Roger W Ferguson
speeches.title: Basel II - a realist's perspective
speeches.reason: The speech covers Basel II capital rules, the US rulemaking process (CP3 and the ANPR), complexity, and competitive equity. It says nothing about interest rates, inflation, or the economic outlook.

speeches.speaker: Mark W Olson
speeches.title: Basel II - its implications for second-tier and community-size banks
speeches.reason: The speech covers how Basel II applies to second-tier and community banks, including costs and benefits, competitive balance and risk-management practices. It says nothing about the outlook for US interest rates, inflation or economic growth.

speeches.speaker: Ben S Bernanke
speeches.title: Will business investment bounce back?
speeches.reason: The speech is mostly an analysis of business investment and does not discuss the policy path directly. It sees a moderate recovery in the second half of 2003 and says policy is 'stimulative', which restates the baseline. It adds a slightly cautious note on persistent managerial pessimism and weak growth abroad.

speeches.speaker: Roger W Ferguson
speeches.title: Basel II - a case study in risk management
speeches.reason: The speech is entirely about Basel II, bank risk management, pro-cyclicality of capital requirements and operational risk. It says nothing about US interest rates, inflation or the economic outlook for monetary policy.

speeches.speaker: Alan Greenspan
speeches.title: Follow-up to the semiannual monetary policy report to the Congress
speeches.reason: Greenspan stresses that business caution may linger and that the outlook will come into focus only gradually. He also warns that 'substantial further disinflation would be an unwelcome development,' which signals concern about low inflation and leans dovish ahead of the May 6 meeting. He still expects a rebound and does not announce a policy change, so the tilt is modest.

speeches.speaker: Susan S Bies
speeches.title: Corporate governance
speeches.reason: The speech is entirely about corporate governance, internal controls, internal audit and Sarbanes-Oxley. It says nothing about inflation, growth or interest rates. For example, it states "At its core, the Sarbanes-Oxley Act is a call to get back to the basics."

speeches.speaker: Alan Greenspan
speeches.title: Corporate governance
speeches.reason: The speech covers corporate governance, derivatives markets, counterparty risk, and disclosure. The only macro remark is a passing note that the economy has been resilient with 'subpar' growth, and it says nothing about the path of rates or inflation.

speeches.speaker: Robert D. McTeer
speeches.title: The Prodigal Son as Central Banker
speeches.reason: McTeer echoes the FOMC's disinflation concern and says growth should be 'boosted substantially,' with a preferred pace 'well north of 4 percent' and no inflation risk from it. He calls deflation risk minor and says policy is already 'front-loaded' and very stimulative, so he stops short of asking for more easing than expected. The tilt is mildly dovish, in line with the committee's easing bias.

speeches.speaker: Roger W Ferguson
speeches.title: Expectations
speeches.reason: Ferguson echoes the FOMC's concern about 'further declines from the already low prevailing level of inflation' and says 'we shall be on guard against such a development.' He sees substantial slack, job losses, and a need for faster demand growth, and says the central bank should work to close the output gap. He also calls deflation 'quite remote,' which tempers the dovish tone, so the speech is a

speeches.speaker: Robert D. McTeer
speeches.title: Commencement Address to Economics Graduates
speeches.reason: This is a humorous commencement speech with only passing economic remarks. He calls the unemployment bulge 'temporary' and mentions 'historically low interest rates' that should lead businesses to invest, so he sees recovery coming without calling for a policy change.

speeches.speaker: Alan Greenspan
speeches.title: The economic outlook

speeches.title: Assessing prospects for economic growth in the United States

He offers no signal of a further cut or of tightening, so the speech mostly restates the baseline outlook. The mix of near-term weakness and a long-run recovery story is balanced.

speeches.speaker: Susan S Bies
speeches.title: Restoring our confidence in bank controls and financial statements
speeches.reason: The speech is about bank supervision, internal controls and audit quality. It touches on bank earnings, calling the economy 'tepid', but says nothing about the outlook for interest rates, inflation or monetary policy.

speeches.speaker: Ben S Bernanke
speeches.title: Some thoughts on monetary policy in Japan
speeches.reason: The speech is about Japanese deflation. It proposes a price-level target, a fix for the BOJ's balance sheet, and monetary-fiscal cooperation. It says nothing about the US economy, US inflation or the path of the fed funds rate, and it opens by saying the views are strictly his own.

speeches.speaker: Roger W Ferguson
speeches.title: Basel II - scope of application in the United States
speeches.reason: The speech is entirely about Basel II capital rules and their scope of application in the US. It does not discuss the outlook for rates, inflation or growth, so it has no bearing on monetary policy.

speeches.speaker: Roger W Ferguson

speeches.speaker: Susan S Bies
speeches.title: Managing business risks
speeches.reason: The speech is about bank risk management, operational risk, accounting and internal controls (FDICIA, Sarbanes-Oxley). It says nothing about the outlook for interest rates, inflation or growth that bears on monetary policy; mentions of record bank earnings and low rates are descriptive only.

speeches.speaker: Roger W Ferguson
speeches.title: Basel II - some issues for implementation
speeches.reason: The speech is entirely about Basel II capital rules, their pro-cyclicality, and how they would apply in the US. It says nothing about the outlook for rates, inflation or growth that bears on monetary policy.

speeches.speaker: Roger W Ferguson
speeches.title: Basel II - discussion of complex issues
speeches.reason: This is Senate testimony on Basel II capital rules for large banks, covering scope of application, cost, competitive equity and operational risk. It says nothing about the outlook for US rates, inflation or growth, so it has no bearing on monetary policy.

speeches.title: Semiannual monetary policy report to the US Congress

He says upside inflation risks remain 'predominant' but also flags the housing correction and subprime stress as risks, and he offers no hint of near-term cuts. That is slightly hawkish against market pricing of easing, though it is largely a restatement of the committee line.

speeches.title: The economic dynamics of global integration
speeches.reason: The speech is about globalization, competitiveness, education, health care, regulation and long-run fiscal sustainability. It describes the economy as performing well ('relatively favorable U.S. economic performance'), but gives no view on inflation, near-term growth or the policy rate. The fiscal remark that the 'U.S. fiscal position is unsustainable' is structural, not a monetary policy signal.

speeches.speaker: Randall S Kroszner
speeches.title: Federal Reserve initiatives to support minority-owned institutions and expand consumer protection

It says nothing about interest rates, inflation, or the economic outlook, so it gives no signal on the policy path.

speeches.speaker: Randall S Kroszner
speeches.title: Renomination to the Board

speeches.speaker: Richard W. Fisher
speeches.title: Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas

speeches.title: Housing, housing finance, and monetary policy

He gives no explicit commitment to cut and stresses uncertainty. Markets already priced in heavy easing, so this was seen as a mild dovish confirmation, and the rest of the speech is historical.

speeches.title: Analyzing and assessing banking crises

It also stresses that the Fed is monitoring markets closely and that US banks are strongly capitalized. It gives no explicit rate signal, so the tilt is only slightly dovish.

speeches.speaker: Frederic S Mishkin

He also says the FOMC "is prepared to act as needed." That is dovish in tone, but he gives no explicit rate signal and keeps "vigilant on inflation," so it largely matches what markets already price.

speeches.title: Developing sustainable capital for community investments

speeches.title: Mortgage delinquencies and foreclosures

speeches.speaker: Randall S Kroszner
speeches.title: Mitigating the impact of foreclosures on neighborhoods
speeches.reason: The speech covers foreclosure mitigation, community development and the Fed's partnership with NeighborWorks America. It says nothing about the outlook for rates, inflation or the economy as it bears on monetary policy.

speeches.speaker: Ben S Bernanke
speeches.title: Liquidity provision by the Federal Reserve
speeches.reason: The speech is about central bank liquidity provision (Bagehot's principles, the TAF, TSLF, PDCF, the Bear Stearns episode) and liquidity regulation and moral hazard. speeches.speaker: Randall S Kroszner
speeches.title: Risk management and Basel II
speeches.reason: The speech covers Basel II implementation, operational risk management, and bank capital rules. It says nothing about interest rates, inflation or the economic outlook that bears on monetary policy.

speeches.speaker: Ben S Bernanke
speeches.title: Risk management in financial institutions

speeches.speaker: Donald L Kohn

speeches.speaker: Donald L Kohn

speeches.speaker: Ben S Bernanke

speeches.title: Financial reform to address systemic risk

speeches.title: Modernizing bank supervision and regulation

speeches.title: American International Group

speeches.speaker: William C Dudley
speeches.title: Oversight of the Federal Government's intervention at American International Group

speeches.title: Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas

speeches.speaker: Elizabeth A Duke
speeches.title: A framework for analyzing bank lending

speeches.speaker: Ben S Bernanke

speeches.speaker: Ben S Bernanke
speeches.title: Financial innovation and consumer protection
speeches.reason: The speech is about financial innovation and consumer protection, covering credit cards, mortgages and overdraft rules. It says nothing about the outlook for interest rates, inflation or the economy that bears on monetary policy.

speeches.speaker: Donald L Kohn
speeches.title: Monetary policy in the financial crisis
speeches.reason: Kohn defends the unconventional easing and says policy could 'entail doing more to ease credit if the economy proves resistant' or reverse actions to forestall inflation. speeches.reason: Bernanke restates the baseline: activity to "bottom out, then to turn up later this year", slack to increase further, and inflation to "move down some". Tentative signs of stabilization offset the dovish tilt, and the rest of the speech covers financial conditions and transparency.

speeches.title: Confronting "too big to fail"

speeches.reason: Bernanke restates the existing guidance ('exceptionally low levels of the federal funds rate at least through late 2014') and the Twist program. He stresses the weak labor market, 'significant downside risks' from Europe, and that the Committee 'is prepared to adjust those holdings as appropriate', which tilts slightly dovish. He gives no clear signal of new easing, so the surprise is small.

speeches.speaker: Richard W. Fisher
speeches.title: Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas
speeches.reason: The speech is about renminbi internationalization and China's financial-sector reform. It says nothing on the US rate path, inflation or the US growth outlook. The only monetary-policy remark is a passing line about keeping the dollar's purchasing power, which carries no signal for policy.

speeches.speaker: Daniel K Tarullo
speeches.title: Shadow banking after the financial crisis
speeches.reason: The speech is about regulatory reform of shadow banking (money market funds, triparty repo, securities lending). It says nothing about the outlook for rates, inflation or growth that bears on monetary policy.

speeches.speaker: FOMC Chair (press conference Q&A)
speeches.title: FOMC press conference: questions and answers
speeches.reason: Bernanke repeatedly says the Fed is prepared to do more, including new asset purchases, if the labor market does not improve. He also stresses the costs and risks of these tools and says they should not be launched lightly. The overall result is a slightly dovish tilt relative to expectations, since he signals no urgency and says further maturity extension is unlikely.

speeches.speaker: Richard W. Fisher
speeches.title: Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas
speeches.reason: This is a historical and anniversary speech about the founding of the Dallas Fed. It covers Dallas winning a Reserve Bank, the bank's early years, and Texas economic growth. It says nothing about the outlook for rates, inflation or the economy that bears on monetary policy.

speeches.speaker: Richard W. Fisher
speeches.title: Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas
speeches.reason: The speech is a personal, biographical talk about Fisher's father and the immigrant experience, given at the Australian American Leadership Dialogue. It says nothing about the outlook for rates, inflation or the economy, or about monetary policy.

speeches.speaker: Ben S Bernanke
speeches.title: Semiannual Monetary Policy Report to the Congress
speeches.reason: Bernanke restates the existing path: low rates through late 2014 and the MEP extension. His emphasis is dovish, citing a weaker outlook, 'significant downside risks to economic growth', and 'frustratingly slow' unemployment declines. He repeats that the Committee 'is prepared to take further action as appropriate' but signals nothing beyond what markets expected.

speeches.speaker: Elizabeth A Duke
speeches.title: Central bank cooperation in times of crisis
speeches.reason: The speech reviews central bank cooperation, swap lines and regulatory coordination, plus Latin American policy. It only recaps past Fed policies, such as the 'late 2014' forward guidance, and says nothing new about the US rate or inflation outlook.

speeches.speaker: Sarah Bloom Raskin
speeches.title: How well is our financial system serving us? Working together to find the high road
speeches.reason: The speech is about bank business models, community banking, and the Volcker Rule. It says nothing about interest rates, inflation, or the economic outlook for monetary policy.

speeches.speaker: Ben S Bernanke
speeches.title: Early childhood education
speeches.reason: The speech is about early childhood education and its long-run economic returns. It says nothing about the outlook for interest rates, inflation, or near-term economic conditions, so it has no bearing on monetary policy.

speeches.speaker: FOMC (statement)
speeches.title: FOMC statement
speeches.reason: The statement keeps the late-2014 guidance and the Twist extension unchanged. It adds a note that the Committee will provide additional accommodation as needed, and it describes slower growth and significant downside risks. The market had priced some chance of immediate new easing and did not get it, so the statement leans slightly dovish with no real surprise. Lacker's hawkish dissent is routine

speeches.speaker: Ben S Bernanke
speeches.title: Economic measurement
speeches.reason: The speech is about economic measurement and well-being metrics (GDP, happiness indices, behavioral economics). It says nothing about the outlook for rates, inflation or monetary policy; the only policy mention is the dual mandate, and the passing note that many households 'continue to struggle' is not a forward-looking policy statement.

speeches.speaker: Ben S Bernanke
speeches.title: Financial education
speeches.reason: The speech is entirely about financial education for students and teachers. It says nothing about the outlook for rates, inflation or the economy that bears on monetary policy.

speeches.speaker: Ben S Bernanke
speeches.title: Monetary policy since the onset of the crisis
speeches.reason: Bernanke defends nontraditional tools as effective and manageable, calls labor market stagnation 'a grave concern', and says the Fed 'will provide additional policy accommodation as needed'. This signals a bias toward further easing (QE3) as likely, though he stops short of committing to a specific action or timing, and notes the higher bar for nontraditional policy.

speeches.speaker: FOMC Chair (press conference Q&A)
speeches.title: FOMC press conference: questions and answers
speeches.reason: Bernanke frames QE3 as open-ended and conditional, says the Fed will do more if the economy is weak, and says it won't rush to tighten even after the recovery strengthens. He reinforces the extended low-rate guidance and says the labor market remains quite weak. speeches.title: Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas

speeches.speaker: Ben S Bernanke
speeches.title: Five questions about the Federal Reserve and monetary policy
speeches.reason: Bernanke restates the September FOMC decisions: open-ended MBS purchases, rates low until at least mid-2015, and accommodation 'for a considerable time after the economy strengthens'. He downplays inflation risk and warns that raising rates now would push unemployment up again, which is a mildly dovish emphasis. He announces no new easing beyond what markets already priced.

speeches.speaker: Elizabeth A Duke
speeches.title: Addressing long-term vacant properties to support neighborhood stabilization
speeches.reason: The speech is about vacant properties and neighborhood stabilization, which is community development. The only monetary policy remark is a closing line that the Fed will 'continue to support recovery through the use of all its policy tools', which restates the existing accommodative stance and gives no new signal on the rate path.

speeches.speaker: Daniel K Tarullo
speeches.title: Financial stability regulation
speeches.reason: The speech is a lecture on Dodd-Frank financial stability regulation: systemic risk capital surcharges, merger review, and shadow banking. It gives no view on the outlook for rates, inflation or growth. The only macro remark is a passing mention that the economy continues to recover 'only slowly'.

speeches.speaker: Duvvuri Subbarao
speeches.title: Quantitative easing - unconventional policy response to the financial crisis
speeches.reason: This is an introductory welcome by the RBI Governor, not a Fed official, praising Bernanke's legacy and summarizing QE and its criticisms. It offers no view on the outlook for US rates, inflation or the economy; it merely restates the existing QE3 commitment.

speeches.speaker: Richard W. Fisher
speeches.title: Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas
speeches.reason: Fisher says little about the policy path but argues monetary policy is not the constraint on hiring. speeches.speaker: Janet L Yellen
speeches.title: Japan in the global economy
speeches.reason: The speech covers global recovery, emerging Asia rebalancing and Japan's fiscal and structural challenges. It makes no forward-looking comments on US rates or policy, only noting that 'very accommodative monetary policies' have not fully offset weak advanced-economy growth.

speeches.speaker: Jeremy C Stein
speeches.title: Evaluating large-scale asset purchases
speeches.reason: Stein firmly backs the September easing: "I firmly believe that this decision was the right one", and he rules out raising rates early to address financial stability concerns. He also stresses diminishing returns and costs from LSAPs, and says the bar for nonconventional policy is higher. That is a mildly hawkish caveat, but it does not change the expected path, so the net tilt is slightly dovish.

speeches.speaker: Ben S Bernanke
speeches.title: US monetary policy and international implications
speeches.reason: Bernanke restates and defends the September easing package: rates exceptionally low until mid-2015, open-ended MBS purchases, and downside risks from Europe. He notes inflation is below target and that unconventional tools carry costs, but he does not signal a path easier than what is already priced, so the tilt is only slightly dovish.

speeches.speaker: FOMC (statement)
speeches.title: FOMC statement
speeches.reason: The October 2012 statement essentially repeats the September QE3 and mid-2015 guidance, so it matches what markets expected. The only hawkish element is Lacker's lone dissent, which is a routine repeat. The statement's small dovish tilt comes from its emphasis on downside risks from global strains and on inflation running at or below 2 percent.

speeches.speaker: Richard W. Fisher
speeches.title: Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas
speeches.reason: This is a welcome address to a US-Mexico development conference, comparing Mexican and US growth, fiscal positions and Mexico's monetary reform history. It says nothing about the US rate path or the FOMC's policy stance; the only US remarks are passing criticism of fiscal imbalances.

speeches.speaker: Elizabeth A Duke
speeches.title: Community banks and mortgage lending
speeches.reason: The speech is about Basel III capital proposals, community bank regulation and mortgage lending data. It says nothing about the outlook for rates, inflation or the economy that bears on monetary policy.

speeches.speaker: Janet L Yellen
speeches.title: Revolution and evolution in central bank communications

speeches.speaker: Ben S Bernanke
speeches.title: Challenges in housing and mortgage markets
speeches.reason: The speech is mostly about housing and mortgage finance. It restates existing policy: the Fed will 'continue actions to put downward pressure on longer-term interest rates until the outlook for the job market improves substantially', and it voices concern about 'stubbornly high' unemployment. This is slightly dovish in emphasis but contains no new path signal.

speeches.speaker: Richard W. Fisher
speeches.title: Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas
speeches.reason: The speech is mostly about regional job growth in the West and Texas versus California, but it includes a mild hawkish caution on the Fed's balance sheet: 'We dare not become the central bank counterpart to Congress by adopting a Buzz Lightyear approach of "To infinity and beyond!" by endlessly purchasing U.S. Treasuries.' It also says inflation and expectations are tame and unemployment is high,

speeches.speaker: Ben S Bernanke
speeches.title: The economic recovery and economic policy
speeches.reason: Bernanke restates the September guidance and open-ended QE: policy will remain 'highly accommodative... for a considerable time after the economic recovery strengthens'. He stresses slack, headwinds and fiscal cliff risks, which tilts slightly dovish, but he announces no change to the expected path.

speeches.speaker: Daniel K Tarullo
speeches.title: Regulation of foreign banking organizations
speeches.reason: The speech is entirely about prudential regulation of foreign banking organizations in the US (intermediate holding companies, capital and liquidity standards). It says nothing about the outlook for rates, inflation or growth, so it has no bearing on monetary policy.

speeches.speaker: Jeremy C Stein
speeches.title: Large-scale asset purchases

speeches.reason: The speech is about industry structure, scale and scope economies, and systemic risk regulation (Glass-Steagall, nondeposit liability caps, long-term debt requirements). It says nothing about monetary policy, inflation, or the economic outlook.

speeches.speaker: FOMC Chair (press conference Q&A)
speeches.title: FOMC press conference: questions and answers
speeches.reason: Bernanke introduced the 6.5% unemployment threshold but says it is consistent with the mid-2015 expectation, and that purchases are a continuation of September. He stresses gradual tightening after liftoff and being 'more proactive now', but also notes costs of a large balance sheet and that purchases would ramp down if the outlook strengthens, so the net tilt is only mildly dovish.

speeches.speaker: Jeremy C Stein
speeches.title: Dollar funding and global banks
speeches.reason: The speech covers dollar funding of global banks, FX swap markets, swap lines and the regulation of foreign banking organizations. It says nothing about the outlook for US rates, inflation or growth. The only policy mention is the FOMC's extension of the swap lines, which is a liquidity facility rather than monetary policy stance.

speeches.speaker: Richard W. Fisher
speeches.title: Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas

He puts the main problem on fiscal and regulatory uncertainty and does not call for a change in the policy path, so the tilt is only slightly hawkish.

speeches.speaker: Janet L Yellen
speeches.title: Interconnectedness and systemic risk - lessons from the financial crisis and policy implications
speeches.reason: The speech covers financial-network research, systemic risk, Basel capital rules and OTC derivatives reform. It says nothing about the outlook for rates, inflation or the economy that bears on monetary policy.

speeches.speaker: Richard W. Fisher
speeches.title: Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas
speeches.reason: The speech is entirely about ending too-big-to-fail banks, Dodd-Frank complexity, and the Dallas Fed's restructuring proposal. It says nothing about the outlook for rates, inflation, or growth. The only monetary reference is that TBTF banks interfere with policy transmission, which is not a policy-path signal.

speeches.speaker: FOMC (statement)

It notes a pause in growth attributed to transitory factors, and downside risks are still cited, which is mildly dovish. George's dissent for tighter policy is a slight hawkish offset, so the net tilt is roughly neutral.

Its only macro remarks are passing ones, such as the interest margin pressure from "a sluggish economy" and the hope that conditions reverse "as the economic recovery gains momentum". These say nothing about the policy path.

speeches.title: Anti-money laundering and the Bank Secrecy Act
speeches.reason: This is testimony on Bank Secrecy Act and anti-money laundering supervision and enforcement, covering OFAC sanctions compliance, cross-border payments and enforcement actions. It says nothing about the outlook for interest rates, inflation or the economy.

This restates the expected accommodative path with a mild dovish tilt and no new signal.

speeches.speaker: Ben S Bernanke
speeches.title: Financial and economic education
speeches.reason: The speech is about financial and economic education programs at the Fed and the need for financial literacy. It mentions the dual mandate only in passing and says nothing about the outlook for rates, inflation or the economy.

speeches.title: Stress testing banks - what have we learned?

It has only a passing remark that the economy is 'significantly stronger than it was four years ago, although conditions are clearly still far from where we would all like them to be', and nothing on the future path of rates or inflation.

speeches.title: Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas

speeches.speaker: Ben S Bernanke
speeches.title: Creating resilient communities
speeches.reason: The speech is about community development and resilience in low-income neighborhoods. It says nothing about the outlook for interest rates, inflation, or monetary policy; its only macro remark is that employment and housing show signs of improving nationally.

speeches.speaker: Janet L Yellen
speeches.title: Panel discussion on "Monetary policy - many targets, many instruments. Where do we stand?"
speeches.reason: Yellen restates the existing guidance and defends accommodation, saying the policy rate should be held 'lower for longer' than conventional rules imply. This is a mild dovish tilt with no change to the expected path.

speeches.speaker: Jeremy C Stein
speeches.title: Regulating large financial institutions
speeches.reason: The speech is entirely about regulating systemically important financial institutions, covering TBTF, capital surcharges, senior debt requirements and corporate governance. It says nothing about the outlook for rates, inflation or the economy that bears on monetary policy.

speeches.speaker: Sarah Bloom Raskin
speeches.title: Aspects of inequality in the recent business cycle
speeches.reason: Raskin links inequality and household deleveraging to a weak, tepid recovery and supports the FOMC's accommodative stance, saying 'accommodative policies of the FOMC...will help the economy continue to gain traction.' She restates the existing path with a mild dovish tilt and signals no change in policy, and she notes that cyclical labor-market gains will do little for inequality.

speeches.speaker: Jeremy C Stein
speeches.title: Liquidity regulation and central banking
speeches.reason: The speech is entirely about liquidity regulation (the Liquidity Coverage Ratio), the lender of last resort, and committed liquidity facilities. It says nothing about the outlook for interest rates, inflation, or the economy that bears on monetary policy.

speeches.speaker: William C Dudley
speeches.title: Opening remarks for the Transatlantic Economic Interdependence and Policy Challenges Conference

speeches.speaker: Daniel K Tarullo
speeches.title: Evaluating progress in regulatory reforms to promote financial stability

The only monetary policy reference is a one-line restatement that 'we continue to foster more-accommodative financial conditions', which gives no new information on the rate path.

speeches.speaker: Ben S Bernanke
speeches.title: Monitoring the financial system
speeches.reason: The speech is about the Fed's financial stability monitoring program: SIFIs, shadow banking, asset markets and the nonfinancial sector. It makes no forward-looking statement on rates, inflation or the growth outlook. speeches.speaker: Ben S Bernanke

speeches.speaker: Ben S Bernanke
speeches.title: The ten suggestions

speeches.speaker: Janet L Yellen
speeches.title: Regulatory landscapes - a US perspective
speeches.reason: The speech is entirely about financial regulation: Basel III, SIFI capital surcharges, resolution regimes and shadow banking. It says nothing about the outlook for US rates, inflation or the economy, so it has no bearing on monetary policy.

speeches.title: Let s move forward - the case for timely implementation of revised capital rules

speeches.speaker: Lael Brainard
speeches.title: The "New Normal" and what it means for monetary policy
speeches.reason: Brainard argues the Phillips curve is flat, the neutral rate is low, and risks are asymmetric, so "the case to tighten policy preemptively is less compelling." She concludes the "asymmetry in risk management... counsels prudence in the removal of policy accommodation," which was a clearly dovish message just before the blackout, when markets were pricing a possible hike.

speeches.speaker: FOMC Chair (press conference Q&A)
speeches.title: FOMC press conference: questions and answers
speeches.reason: Yellen held rates but said the case for a hike had strengthened, that most participants expect one hike this year, and that every meeting including November is live. She also stressed that the economy has more room to run, that the neutral rate is lower, and that inflation is below target, which offsets the hawkish signals. Overall this confirms the expected path with a very slight hawkish tilt.

speeches.title: Next steps in the evolution of stress testing
speeches.reason: The speech covers stress testing and CCAR reforms, including the proposed stress capital buffer, GSIB surcharges and transparency. It says nothing about interest rates, inflation, employment or the economic outlook for monetary policy.

speeches.speaker: Stanley Fischer
speeches.title: Why study economics?
speeches.reason: This is a convocation address on why to study economics. It covers labor force participation, economic mobility and diversity in the economics profession. speeches.speaker: Janet L Yellen
speeches.title: Supervision and regulation
speeches.reason: The testimony before the House Financial Services Committee covers stress testing, the stress capital buffer, resolution planning, TLAC and community bank tailoring. It says nothing about interest rates, inflation or the economic outlook that bears on monetary policy.

speeches.speaker: Jerome H Powell
speeches.title: Trends in community bank performance over the past 20 years
speeches.reason: The speech reviews trends in community bank numbers and performance, then covers regulatory burden relief and research plans. Its only macro mention is a passing reference to 'very low interest rates and a post-crisis expansion that has been slower than usual' as explaining weak new bank entry. That gives no signal on the future path of policy.

speeches.speaker: Janet L Yellen
speeches.title: Brief remarks
speeches.reason: The speech is only about diversity and inclusion at the Federal Reserve and in banking. It says nothing about interest rates, inflation, employment or the economic outlook, so it has no monetary policy content.

speeches.speaker: William C Dudley
speeches.title: Remarks at the 40th Annual Central Banking Seminar
speeches.reason: Dudley mostly gives a general overview of central banking, but he adds a risk-management argument: if unconventional policy is less effective at the zero lower bound, 'the more cautious one would be in the process of removing accommodation.' This leans slightly dovish toward gradualism. He does not change the expected path, and he notes that he does not think expansions die of old age.

speeches.speaker: Jeffrey M. Lacker
speeches.title: Economic Outlook, October 2016
speeches.reason: Lacker argues benchmarks imply a policy rate of "1 ½ percent or more by now" and calls for a "strong case" for raising rates, with pre-emptive hikes to avoid more drastic action later. He is the known hawkish dissenter, so this is largely a repeat of his position. It is still more hawkish than the committee and market path, which implies a much slower pace.

speeches.speaker: Jeffrey M. Lacker
speeches.title: Does Federal Reserve Governance Need Reform?
speeches.reason: The speech is about Fed governance structure, covering the Fed's founding, Reserve Bank boards, bankers' conflicts of interest and policy independence. speeches.speaker: Lael Brainard
speeches.title: Distributed ledger technology - implications for payments, clearing, and settlement

speeches.speaker: Stanley Fischer

He calls September a 'close call' and sees the economy near full employment. He also stresses gradualism ('little risk of falling behind the curve') and that policy is 'not on a preset course', which offsets most of the hawkish tilt.

speeches.reason: The speech is about financial regulation, covering systemic risk, shadow banking, SIFIs, and how to teach and research the subject. It says nothing about the outlook for interest rates, inflation, or the economy.

The tone is mildly dovish because he sees no need to tighten for financial stability reasons, but he gives no forward guidance.

He warns unemployment could "drift below its long-run sustainable level" and push inflation above target without further hikes. He stays within a gradual framework, which limits the surprise.

She does note that faster fiscal-driven slack absorption could mean quicker adjustment, and that domestic risks are "closer to being balanced". The net effect is a mildly dovish tilt on a gradual path.

speeches.speaker: Janet L Yellen

The net read was dovish relative to markets, which priced hikes next year, and he expected inflation to fall by Q2/Q3.

speeches.title: The Economic Mixdown
speeches.reason: Williams says inflation at about 3-1/2% is 'simply too high' and 'the risk to achieving price stability is dialed up,' and notes that supply-side risks are skewed to the upside. He gives no explicit hike signal and no path guidance, and he is relatively sanguine on expectations, wages and tariffs, and projects inflation falling to just above 2% next year. That leaves a hawkish lean rather than a call for a tighter path.
speeches.quote: So, the risk to maximum employment is dialed down, but the risk to achieving price stability is dialed up.
speeches.path: Markets price some hikes: the 6-month bill is 38bp and the 2-year 75bp above the 3.88% target, which implies roughly one to three hikes over the next year or two.
speeches.moves: 2y yield -0.4bp (approx.); US dollar index +0.10%; S&P 500 futures -0.20%

sources.y2: FRED, series DGS2 (Board of Governors H.15)

anchors.speaker: Stephen I. Miran
anchors.title: Regulations, the Supply Side, and Monetary Policy
anchors.path: As of January 2026, after cuts in late 2025 the fed funds rate sits near 3.50-3.75%, with the FOMC and markets expecting a slow, gradual easing (about one or two more cuts in 2026).
anchors.reason: Miran argues that deregulation is a large positive supply shock that lowers prices and widens the output gap, so it "supports a more accommodative stance of monetary policy." He says policy has been "tighter than it should have been" and that he expects to press this view with FOMC colleagues, which implies a faster and larger easing path than the committee expects.

anchors.speaker: Christopher J. Waller
anchors.title: Statement by Governor Christopher J. Waller
anchors.path: After three cuts in 2025 and a hold at the January 2026 meeting, the FOMC and markets expect a pause with gradual further easing later, roughly one or two cuts in 2026.
anchors.reason: Waller dissented in favor of a 25bp cut, saying "economic data make it clear to me further easing is needed" and that policy is still 50 to 75bp above neutral. He stresses a weak labor market with "zero" 2025 job growth, a significant risk of deterioration, and tariff inflation that can be looked through. This is a clearly easier path than the committee's hold.

anchors.speaker: Michelle W. Bowman
anchors.title: Outlook for the Economy and Monetary Policy
anchors.path: As of January 2026, after three 25bp cuts to 3.50-3.75%, the FOMC is expected to pause at the late-January meeting, with perhaps one or two more cuts later in 2026.
anchors.reason: Bowman says the labor market is fragile and policy is still 'moderately restrictive.' She argues the Fed should 'remain ready to adjust policy to bring it closer to neutral' and should avoid signaling a pause, which is more dovish than the expected pause. She also sees inflation falling toward 2% once tariff effects fade, and says risks are not symmetric and tilt toward employment.

anchors.speaker: Philip N. Jefferson
anchors.title: Economic Outlook and Supply-Side (Dis)Inflation Dynamics
anchors.path: FOMC paused in late January 2026 after 175bp of cuts since mid-2024; markets expect a data-dependent, meeting-by-meeting path with perhaps a couple more cuts later in 2026.
anchors.reason: Jefferson supported holding rates, says policy is 'broadly in the range of estimates of the neutral rate' and 'well positioned,' with a meeting-by-meeting, data-dependent approach. He leans slightly dovish by expecting disinflation to resume, treating tariffs as a one-time price-level shift, and saying there is 'more leeway' without 'precautionary monetary policy restraint.' He also notes that downside risks to employment remain, but acknowledges upside inflation risks and a possibly higher neutral rate.

anchors.speaker: John Williams
anchors.title: A Few Words for the New Year
anchors.path: After 75bp of cuts in 2025, the FOMC is expected to hold near-term, with perhaps one or two more cuts in 2026 as inflation peaks in H1 and the labor market stabilizes.
anchors.reason: Williams says policy is 'well positioned' after 75bp of cuts, with the stance moved 'closer to neutral' and risks 'in better balance'. He gives a favorable outlook (inflation peaking at 2-3/4 to 3 percent, then falling; unemployment stabilizing) and stays data dependent. He signals neither further cuts nor hikes.

anchors.speaker: Jerome H. Powell
anchors.title: FOMC press conference, 18 March 2026
anchors.path: Hold at 3.5-3.75% in March, with the SEP median still showing one cut in 2026 (3.4% at year-end) and another in 2027 (3.1%), conditional on tariff disinflation.
anchors.reason: Powell holds rates and leaves the median SEP path unchanged, but he leans slightly hawkish. He says the 'look through' question 'doesn't really arise until we have kind of checked that box' on tariff progress, notes movement toward fewer cuts, says a rate increase 'did come up', and says 'if we don't see that progress, then you won't see the rate cut'. He also stresses downside labor risks and says nobody knows how the oil shock will play out, which keeps the stance balanced.

anchors.speaker: Lisa D. Cook
anchors.title: Economic Outlook
anchors.path: FOMC held the policy rate steady in late January 2026 after three cuts in 2025; markets expect a pause with perhaps a couple of further cuts later in 2026, data-dependent.
anchors.reason: Cook says "I see risks as tilted toward higher inflation" and supported holding the rate until she sees "stronger evidence that inflation is moving sustainably back down to target." She also stresses credibility and dismisses weak sentiment as not signaling slack that demand-side policy can fix. She stays balanced by noting labor market risks and some optimism on inflation, and she does not call for hikes.

anchors.speaker: Beth Hammack
anchors.title: Trimming the Sails: Communicating My Reaction Function
anchors.path: The speech implies the FOMC holds a restrictive stance, with markets pricing rates on hold or modestly higher as inflation stays elevated (headline PCE 3.4%, core 3.0%).
anchors.reason: Hammack says inflation risks are skewed to the upside, pressures are broad and persistent, and an inflationary mindset may be taking hold. She sees the labor market as stable, financial conditions as neutral, and the economy as able to handle 'a tighter hand on the tiller.' She favors 'frequent smaller adjustments' and says elevated inflation could mean 'pointing the bow of monetary policy rates toward an even higher latitude.' She stops short of an explicit call for hikes, so the score is not higher.

anchors.speaker: Lorie Logan
anchors.title: Opening remarks for moderated conversation at The University of Texas at El Paso
anchors.path: FOMC and markets appear to expect policy on hold at the current rate for now, with no near-term change and no hike clearly priced in.
anchors.reason: Logan says inflation is "taking too long to return" to 2%, that it is likely trending only to the "mid 2's", and that "monetary policy is not restraining the economy." She is "increasingly concerned that higher interest rates could be necessary later this year," which is an explicit tightening bias beyond a hold. She hedges by noting that decisions call for debate and by saying she respects her colleagues' views, so the score stops short of the top of the hawkish range.

anchors.speaker: Jeff Schmid
anchors.title: Agriculture, the Economy, and the Kansas City Fed
anchors.path: The FOMC is presumed to be on hold at a roughly neutral-to-modestly-restrictive rate, with no near-term hikes priced in and inflation expected to ease gradually.
anchors.reason: Schmid says his focus is 'squarely on inflation that remains too high', dismisses the idea that supply shocks are transitory, and says he does not see policy as restrictive given strong demand. He concludes that getting inflation to 2 percent 'will require tighter policy', an explicit call for hikes beyond the expected hold.
